ai.literal: Folly that which is called one thing, what if asked, harm taking, benefit to go letting go.
ai.translation: If one asks what that single thing called folly is, it is taking hold of what is harmful and letting go of what is beneficial.
ai.modern: பேதைமை என்று சொல்லப்படும் ஒரு தன்மை யாது என்று கேட்டால், அது தனக்குத் துன்பம் தருவனவற்றை ஏற்றுக்கொண்டு, நன்மை தருவனவற்றைத் நழுவவிடுவது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the core nature of folly. The poet asks a rhetorical question about what constitutes folly, and answers it directly. Folly is the lack of discernment that leads a person to actively embrace things that bring harm (ētam) while letting go of things that bring true benefit (ūtiyam). A foolish person acts against their own self-interest, choosing ruin over prosperity.

ai.literal: Among all follies, the folly is excessive desire towards that which is not proper, doing it upon oneself.
ai.translation: The greatest folly of all follies is the obsessive desire to perform actions that are not worthy of oneself.
ai.modern: அறிவீனங்கள் எல்லாவற்றிலும் மிகப்பெரிய அறிவீனம் என்பது, தனக்குத் தகுதி இல்லாத செயல்களின் மேல் ஆசைப்பட்டு அவற்றைச் செய்வதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the ultimate form of folly. Among all foolish acts, the most foolish is having a strong desire (காதன்மை) for things that are not proper or suitable (கையல்ல) for one's character or capability, and attempting to perform them (தன்கட் செயல்). Here, 'கை' refers to proper conduct or capability, and 'கையல்ல' means actions that are inappropriate or beyond one's capacity. True wisdom lies in knowing one's limits and duties, whereas folly drives a person to obsess over and pursue what is unfit for them.

ai.literal: Shamelessness, not seeking, absence of affection, not cherishing even one of anything, is the conduct of a fool.
ai.translation: Shamelessness, lack of inquiry, absence of affection, and neglecting to cherish anything of value are the characteristics of a fool.
ai.modern: வெட்கப்பட வேண்டியவற்றிற்கு வெட்கப்படாமல் இருத்தல், நன்மைகளை ஆராய்ந்து நாடாமல் இருத்தல், அன்பு இல்லாமல் இருத்தல், எதனையும் போற்றிப் பாதுகாக்காமல் இருத்தல் ஆகியவையே அறிவிலியின் செயல்களாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the core behaviors that characterize a fool. The poet lists four distinct traits: shamelessness for wrong actions, a failure to seek or inquire into what is beneficial, a complete lack of affection towards others, and the failure to cherish or protect anything of value. The word 'nār' literally means fiber, but in classical Tamil, it is a well-known metaphor for the binding force of love or affection, which fits perfectly in this context of human relationships. By combining these four negative traits, the couplet provides a comprehensive definition of folly in action.

ai.literal: Having studied, and having understood, and having expounded to others, oneself not self-controlled, than that fool, greater fools there are none.
ai.translation: There are no greater fools than those who, despite having studied, understood, and taught others, do not practice self-control themselves.
ai.modern: நூல்களைப் படித்து, அவற்றின் பொருளை உணர்ந்து, பிறருக்கும் எடுத்துச் சொல்லியும், தான் அதன்படி அடங்கி நடக்காத பேதையை விடப் பெரிய பேதையர் யாரும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the ultimate form of foolishness. A person might read many books, grasp their deep meanings, and even teach these values to others. However, if they fail to control their own desires and actions according to that knowledge, their learning is entirely useless. The poet emphasizes that there is no greater fool than someone who possesses knowledge but fails to live by it.

ai.literal: In a single birth, the action that a fool performs is a hell in which he himself, entering, will sink for all seven births.
ai.translation: The deed that a fool performs in a single birth is a hell into which he himself will enter and sink for all seven births.
ai.modern: ஒரு பிறவியில் அறிவிலி செய்யும் செயலானது, அவன் ஏழு பிறவிகளிலும் தானே புகுந்து மூழ்கிக் கிடக்கும் நரகமாக மாறும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns of the long-lasting consequences of foolish actions. A fool performs a deed in a single lifetime without foresight or wisdom. This single action becomes like a deep, miry hell into which he himself must enter and sink repeatedly across all seven of his future births. The poet emphasizes that the suffering is self-inflicted and enduring, highlighting the gravity of foolishness.

ai.literal: If a fool who does not know the proper method of action undertakes a task, will it only fail? He will also wear fetters.
ai.translation: If a fool who does not know the proper way of doing things undertakes a task, not only will the task fail, but he will also end up wearing fetters.
ai.modern: செயல் செய்யும் முறையை அறியாத அறிவிலி ஒரு செயலை மேற்கொண்டால், அச்செயல் கெடுவது மட்டுமன்றி, அவன் விலங்கையும் (சிறைத்தண்டனையையும்) பூண நேரிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes the double disaster that occurs when an ignorant person (பேதை) attempts a task without knowing the proper methods (கையறியா). First, the undertaking itself is bound to fail (பொய்படும்). Second, the consequences of his foolish actions will not stop at mere failure; he will also face punishment or imprisonment, metaphorically described as wearing fetters (புனைபூணும்). The word 'ஒன்றோ' (is it only one?) highlights that failure is not the only outcome, emphasizing the compounding nature of a fool's mistakes.

ai.literal: Strangers to be satisfied, one's own people will starve, when a fool great wealth acquires.
ai.translation: When a fool acquires great wealth, strangers will feast to their heart's content while his own relatives starve.
ai.modern: ஒரு அறிவிலி பெரும் செல்வத்தை அடையும் போது, அவனுடைய உறவினர்கள் பசியால் வாட, அந்நியர்கள் அந்தச் செல்வத்தை முழுமையாக அனுபவிப்பார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the tragic misdirection of resources when a fool gains wealth. The word 'தமர்' refers to one's own family and relatives, who naturally deserve support, while 'ஏதிலார்' refers to strangers or outsiders. Instead of helping those close to him, the fool squanders his fortune on outsiders who flatter him, leaving his own kin to starve ('பசிப்பர்'). The term 'கடை' is used here in a temporal sense to mean 'when' or 'at the time of' acquiring wealth.

ai.literal: Like a madman becoming intoxicated indeed is a fool if he obtains a possession in his hand.
ai.translation: A fool obtaining a possession in his hand is like a madman becoming intoxicated.
ai.modern: மனநலம் குன்றிய ஒருவன் மதுவருந்தி வெறி கொள்வதைப் போன்றது, அறிவிலி தன் கையில் ஏதேனும் ஒரு செல்வத்தைப் பெறுவது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares a fool who acquires wealth to a madman who gets drunk. A person who is already mentally unstable (மையல் ஒருவன்) will lose all remaining restraint and act wildly if they consume alcohol (களித்தற்று). Similarly, a fool (பேதை), who already lacks wisdom and self-control, becomes completely reckless and arrogant when they acquire a possession (உடைமை) in their hand. The analogy highlights how sudden fortune does not improve a fool, but rather amplifies their inherent foolishness and makes them dangerous.

ai.literal: Greatly pleasant is the friendship of fools; at the time of separation, pain-giving one thing is not.
ai.translation: The friendship of fools is highly pleasant, because when they part, there is not a single thing that causes pain.
ai.modern: அறிவிலாதவர்களின் நட்பு மிகவும் இனிமையானது; ஏனெனில், அவர்கள் பிரியும்போது துன்பம் தருவது ஒன்றும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses irony to describe the friendship of foolish people. The poet states that their friendship is highly pleasant, but the reason is humorous: when the friendship ends and they part ways, it causes absolutely no sorrow or pain. Normally, parting from a true friend is painful, but parting from a fool brings only relief. Thus, the lack of pain during separation is what makes their friendship 'pleasant' in a satirical sense.

ai.literal: Unwashed foot inside the bed having placed is like, noble people's assembly a fool entering.
ai.translation: A fool entering the assembly of the noble is like stepping onto a clean bed with unwashed feet.
ai.modern: கழுவாத காலைப் படுக்கையினுள் வைப்பதைப் போன்றது, சான்றோர்களின் அவையினுள் அறிவிலி நுழைவது.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a vivid everyday analogy to illustrate the discordance of ignorance in a refined setting. Entering a clean bed with dirty, unwashed feet instantly soils and ruins the purity of the sleeping space. Similarly, when an ignorant person enters an assembly of wise and noble scholars, their presence and unrefined behavior disrupt the intellectual harmony of the gathering. The poet highlights that a fool's intrusion is not just out of place, but actively defiles the dignity of a noble space.
